                                        Preface

Thomas F. Green (Green), a pro se’ intervenor, presents this filing in good faith and
with factually sound backing. Green is not an attorney and is inexperienced in
preparing and filing this Reply Brief on Remand: it is yet another of his first rodeos
in these proceedings. Where Green offers conclusions of fact or law, it is done with
care and a reasonable understanding of the particular issues. Perfection is not the
standard and is not asserted.

Accordingly, deference and forbearance regarding the form of the Brief is humbly
invited and will be welcomed and much appreciated. It is presumed the SOAH will
view the facts to be of higher importance than an attorney-like presentation of
them. Green’s reply, that of a “lay person” (as the Applicants call the intervenor
witnesses), has immense merit based on the evidentiary record and his review of it.
Green’s Reply Brief on Remand (this Brief) will endeavor to use the “plain
language” professed to be used many times by the Applicants in their earlier filed
Exceptions. This plain language is consistent with Green’s reasonable reading of
the related laws and statutes.

Green is not accusing anyone and is not asserting wrongdoing by anyone. Green is
asking the questions the Law under which he practices oblige him to ask when
significant concerns regarding the Practice of Engineering and protection of the
Public arise.

Engineers have the entrusted duty to protect the health, safety, property, and
welfare of the public. No other profession has this elevated duty to the public,
borne out of the 1937 New London School tragedy. Green’s experience has
demonstrated this elevated duty is implicit within his practice experience.

This Brief is solidly anchored by Green’s 45 years of Professional Engineering
Experience. Green is well-schooled and well-experienced in the Practice of
Engineering, including the Laws, Statutes, and Codes that define the profession, its
duties, and its ethics. These Standards exist for Texas as well as nationally.

The Applicants have the burden of proof, and their brief answers the wrong
question: it recites and relies upon institutional planning history while leaving the
project-specific need, timing, alternatives, environmental, and procedural failures
unaddressed.



                                          4
 The evidentiary record does not support handing the Applicants the State’s heavy
hammer of eminent domain on a record so thin and deficient.
This is the heart of the matter. The Commission may grant this CCN only on
findings of fact supported by credible substantial evidence in this record, and the
burden of producing that credible substantial evidence rests squarely and solely on
the Applicants, not on the landowners forced to defend their and their posterity’s
property.
It should be noted that Green has, out of time necessity, constrained his Reply Brief
on Remand Issue No. 11 as cited below.

This Brief is not an “easy read.” Please take care in its review.

If ever… if EVER… CCNs are not to be approved, the ones in Import Path 2, in
Dockets 59475 and 59182, are such CCNs. Approval of these CCNs would be
tantamount to simply saying the proceedings are irrelevant. The only accountable
and responsible decision for Texans is to deny and to expeditiously re-evaluate.
This plea has been that of Mr. Green’s literally from the start. It is unequivocally
underpinned by the record that has been developed.


                                   End of Preface

 1.0. The Questions Before Us
Green has 45 years of active professional engineering in responsible charge. He
has invested an estimated 1500 hours on the Permian Basin Reliability Plan and its
transmission line CCNs in the last 14 months. He has offered direct testimony,
briefs, and public comment testimony before the PUC, before the Senate
Committee on Business and Commerce, and before the House Committee on State
Affairs. He is deeply acquainted with the duties, laws, and ethics of the engineers,
including. how those laws are applied to public works. He is qualified to offer this
Brief.

To his knowledge, the documents in Dockets 59182 and 59475 that he has
submitted are the only ones bearing a professional engineering seal and the
authenticity and accountability of anything engineering.

As more and more has been learned about the PBRP and the CCN process, there
has been an underlying question gnawing at Green: how is it that the largest
electrical transmission line build out in the history of Texas, larger by 5X the
previous largest, is to be implemented based on documents that would appear to be
absent authenticity and accountability, and that does not comply with state or
federal standards?

Green is mot naïve of the inescapable political influences that come with the PUC,
the SOAH, and the TBPELS all being Executive Branch agencies. He must simply
trust that those influences do not influence the review and findings related to this
Brief and the subject CCNs, and that the Public protection obligations of the PUC
he SOAH, and the TBPELS will override political influences.

Pertinent elements of Green’s research related to the above questions are presented
in following sections of this Brief.

1.1. Question Set No. 1. Eight questions in set one relate to the PUC Remand
   Preliminary Order Issue 11:

   "11. Are the proposed transmission facilities necessary to meet state or federal
   reliability standards?"

   In order to respond to Issue 11, one must first identify the subject standards,
   ascertain what analyses are required to meet the standards, and provide a
   reasonable conclusion as to whether or not those analyses were properly
                                          6
    performed and documented. Green’s treatment of Issue 11 focuses on analysis
   of a relevant part of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation
   (NERC) requirements.

1.1.1. Do the requirements of NERC TPL- 001-0 5.1 identify analysis that require
       or expect electrical or other disciplines of engineering?

1.1.2. Do the analyses of ERCOT in its Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP),
       it’s 2024 Regional Transmission Plan (RTP), and it’s 2025 RTP include
       engineering works as identified by Texas law?

1.1.3. Do the analyses of ERCOT in the PBRP, the 2024 RTP, and the 2025 RTP
       (the Plans) include engineering works as described by the National Council
       of engineering Examiners and Surveying (NCEES), thereby validating the
       requirements of Texas law with the model codes of this national
       organization?

1.1.4. Does ERCOT assert that these Plans were derived using engineering?

1.1.5. If ERCOT asserts it’s Plans are based on Engineering, is it required or
       expected to be registered as a firm that performs professional engineering?

1.1.6. Are the above Plans required or expected to contain the authenticity and the
       accountability of engineering works?

1.1.7. Is the SOAH obliged to refer apparent engineering licensure and
       accountability questions to the TBPELS for investigation?

1.1.8. Is a state agency (e.g., The PUC) obliged to deny an application for Public
       Work infrastructure that should be, but is not authenticated by a professional
       engineer in responsible charge pursuant to state law?

Green’s research and findings result in all of the eight questions above being
answered in the affirmative. Accordingly, the PUCT is obliged to DENY the
applications for CCNs in dockets 59182 and 59475.

1.2.   The other set of questions.

1.2.1. If Green’s research and findings are proven to yield incorrect conclusions by
       the SOAH, what does that mean?
                                          7
 1.2.1.1.       Does it mean the largest electrical transmission infrastructure
       addition in Texas history is allowed to proceed based upon un-authenticated
       reports of purported engineering that are anonymous regarding engineering
       responsible charge?

1.2.1.2.      Does it mean that an absence of accountability to process, accuracy,
       or validity can nonetheless be the foundation for public works affecting:
       health, safety, and environmental integrity; thousands of landowners; and
       every ratepayer served by the ERCOT grid?

1.2.1.3.     Does it mean that the heavy hammer of eminent domain can be
       wielded even in the absence of proven need?

If SOAH’s answer to these three questions is also in the affirmative, meaning that
if such a contrary conclusion to that reached by Green in 1.1 above is reached, then
the question becomes what is the purpose and usefulness of the Texas
Engineering Practices Act and the TBPELS? Are the TEPA and TBPELS not
therefore moot?

1.3. If SOAH’s accepts these Plans as credible substantial evidence to build
   Import Path 2, Green opines that the entire protective premise set by the 1937
   New London School tragedy is undermined and the protection mandated by the
   Texas Engineering Practices Act is voided. This result would mean that State
   entities would not themselves have to abide by the laws the State requires others
   to follow.

.

 2.0. Background of Questions and Answers
2.1. Scope of Preliminary Order Issue 11 and Applicants’ Response

On September 18, 2026, the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission)
remanded Docket No. 59475 to the State Office of Administrative Hearings
(SOAH) to resolve two questions that the original Proposal for Decision (PFD) did
not acceptably address: Preliminary Order Issue 11 and Preliminary Order Issue
13. On September 22, 2026, the Administrative Law Judges (ALJs) issued SOAH
Order No. 35 (Item No. 6597), confirming that the evidentiary record remains
closed and establishing a schedule for briefing.

This Brief addresses Preliminary Order Issue 11, directing a specific factual and
legal inquiry:

"Are the proposed transmission facilities necessary to meet state or federal
reliability standards?"

Under Texas Utilities Code (PURA) § 37.056(c)(4)(D), an applicant seeking an
amendment to a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity (CCN) must establish
that the proposed facilities are necessary to meet state or federal reliability
standards. In this proceeding, Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA
Transmission Services Corporation (Applicants) propose constructing the 765 kV
Import Path 2: the Bell County East to Big Hill (Docket 59475); and Big Hill to
Sand Lake (Docket 59182).

In their initial briefs on remand, the Applicants attempt to answer Issue 11 by
relying on system-wide regional planning reports issued by the ERCOT: the July
2024 PBRP, the 2024 Regional Transmission Plan (RTP), early modeling releases
of the 2025 RTP, and the precursor PBRP. The Applicants argue that because
ERCOT identified long-term load expansion in the Permian Basin, any
transmission line identified within an ERCOT regional plan is automatically
"necessary" to meet reliability standards under PURA § 37.056.

Such a position is logically, technically, and legally flawed.

Demonstrating necessity under an enforceable reliability standard requires
competent, verified engineering proof that this specific 765-kV facility is required
to prevent an identified violation of an enforceable state or federal reliability
standard. The Applicants failed to present Import Path 2 project-specific
engineering proof in the evidentiary record.
                                          9
 The institutional studies (the Plans) upon which the Applicants rely constitute
unauthenticated, unsealed engineering reports produced by an unregistered
corporate entity. Such reliance is a reasonable and direct violation of the Texas
Engineering Practice Act (TEPA) and the mandatory rules of the Texas Board of
Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors (TBPELS). Because the evidentiary
record is closed, the Applicants cannot cure these evidentiary defects.

Issue 11 must be answered in the negative.

2.2    NERC Mandates

Evaluating whether a transmission line is necessary to meet federal reliability
standards requires examining North American Electric Reliability Corporation
(NERC) Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1 ("Transmission System Planning
Performance Requirements") and its supporting Modeling, Data, and Analysis
(MOD) standards.

Federal reliability compliance is not an abstract policy projection; it is a
mandatory, calculations-driven engineering process governed by federal law
pursuant to 16 U.S.C. 824o. That statute’s sole purpose is to enforce highly
technical math and physics-based engineering standards across the nation’s power
grid..

2.2.1. Requirement R1 of NERC TPL-001-5.1 obligates the Planning Coordinator
       (ERCOT) and Transmission Planners to maintain mathematical system
       models of the interconnected transmission network. The maintenance of
       these models carries the implicit requirement that the models use data
       consistently throughout the respective grid. These models must represent
       projected system conditions, real and reactive load demands, generation
       resources, safe operating limits,and physical transmission topologies (i.e.,
       engineering) consistent with data submittals mandated by NERC Standard
       MOD-032-1.

2.2.2. Requirement R2 requires planners to conduct comprehensive steady-state
       power-flow simulations, dynamic angular stability analyses, and short-
       circuit interrupting duty calculations across a wide range of contingency
       Planning Events P0 through P7 (i.e., engineering). Planners must stress
       system models through sensitivity analyses that vary real and reactive load
       forecasts, dispatch patterns, and transfer levels (again, engineering).


                                         10
 2.2.3. Requirements R5 and R6 dictate that the planner establish quantitative
       criteria for steady-state bus voltage limits, transient voltage recovery, and
       system instability thresholds, including cascading failures and uncontrolled
       islanding (i.e., engineering).

2.2.4. Requirements R2.7 and R2.8 require that whenever simulations demonstrate
       thermal overloads or voltage instability, the planning entity must develop a
       formal Corrective Action Plan (CAP). A CAP specifies the precise physical
       modification, replacement, or installation of high-voltage transmission
       lines, transformers, and switchgear necessary to maintain bulk electric
       system performance within safe physical margins (again, engineering).

2.2.5. Complementing these requirements:

2.2.5.1. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Standard MOD-033-1
         mandates the empirical validation of dynamic and steady-state planning
         models by benchmarking simulated system responses against actual
         physical telemetry recorded during grid events (again, engineering).
2.2.5.2. In Ponderosa Power LLC v. Northwestern Corporation (FERC 61.156,
         2025, Docket No. EL24-147-0000), the Commission identifies the use of
         engineering judgment when conducting interconnection studies.

2.2.6. The answer to the first question, “Do the requirements of NERC TPL-
       001-0 5.1 identify analysis that require or expect electrical or other
       disciplines of engineering?” is yes.

2.3.   Statutory Practice of Engineering

These technical operations fall clearly within the statutory definition of the practice
of engineering under Texas law. Texas Occupations Code § 1001.003(c) provides:

2.3.1. "(c) The practice of engineering includes: (1) consultation, investigation,
       evaluation, analysis, planning, engineering for program management,
       providing an expert engineering opinion or testimony, engineering for
       testing or evaluating materials for construction or other engineering use, and
       mapping; . . . [and] (10) a service, design, analysis, or other work performed
       for a public or private entity in connection with a utility, structure, building,
       machine, equipment, process, system, work, project, or industrial or
       consumer product or equipment of a mechanical, electrical, electronic,
       chemical, hydraulic, pneumatic, geotechnical, or thermal nature."

                                           11
 2.3.2. Executing contingency calculations, differential equation dynamic stability
       simulations, short-circuit current determinations, and bus voltage vector
       calculations for an interconnected 765-kV alternating-current network
       requires applying physical, mathematical, and electrical engineering
       principles. Preparing a CAP that dictates the physical parameters of high-
       voltage transmission lines to prevent thermal overloads and cascading grid
       collapse constitutes electrical utility engineering under Texas Occupations
       Code § 1001.003(c)(10).

2.3.3. The distinction between general planning and professional engineering was
       addressed directly by TBPELS in Policy Advisory Opinion No. 2 regarding
       Metropolitan Transportation Planning (EAOR 2, approved May 18, 2005).
       In that advisory, the Board examined whether high-level planning studies
       conducted by regional governmental bodies constitute engineering. The
       Board determined that while broad socioeconomic data gathering,
       population forecasting, and speculative land-use planning do not constitute
       engineering, any analytical activity that evaluates the physical capacity,
       structural dimensions, operational safety, or physical network performance
       of a public infrastructure facility constitutes the practice of engineering and
       must be performed by or under the direct supervision of a licensed
       Professional Engineer.

2.3.4. Applied to bulk power transmission, macro-economic projections of oilfield
       development or data center growth in the Permian Basin may begin as
       general demographic forecasting. The moment those economic forecasts are
       translated into AC load-flows, impedance ratings, conductors sizing,
       congestion forecasts, thermal, reactive and safe power delivery, voltage
       stability thresholds, or physical 765-kV line specifications to prevent grid
       instability, the work solidly enters the regulated practice of engineering
       under Texas law and TBPELS precedent,

2.3.5. This principle is reinforced at the national level by the National Council of
       Examiners for Engineering and Surveying (NCEES). The NCEES Model
       Law 110.20 A.3 explicitly includes within the definition of engineering
       "providing planning, studies, designs, design coordination, drawings,
       specifications, and other technical submissions" for systems that affect
       public welfare.


                                          12
 2.3.6. NCEES Model Law § 110.20 E defines "Responsible Charge" as direct
       control and personal supervision of engineering work, requiring the author to
       be capable of answering all technical questions and assuming full
       professional liability. Both Texas law and national model engineering
       standards classify transmission grid planning and reliability analyses as
       the regulated practice of engineering.

2.3.7. Because the planning studies supporting Import Path 2 constitute
       engineering, both the corporate entity issuing them and the individuals
       preparing them must comply with TEPA. Subchapter B of Chapter 1001 of
       the Texas Occupations Code confirms that ERCOT is not exempt from firm
       registration, nor are its engineers exempt from signing and sealing technical
       reports.

2.3.8. The answer to the second question, “Do the analyses of ERCOT in its
       Permian basin reliability plan (PBRP), its 2024 Regional Transmission Plan
       (RTP), and its 2025 RTP include engineering works as identified by Texas
       law?” is yes.

2.3.9. The answer to the third question, “Do the analyses of ERCOT in the
       PBRP, the 2024 RTP, and the 2025 RTP include engineering works as
       described by the national council of engineering examiners (NCEE), thereby
       validating the requirements of Texas law with the model codes of this
       national organization?” is yes.

2.3.10.     The answer to the sixth question, “Are the above Plans required or
      expected to contain the authenticity and the accountability of engineering
      works?” is yes.

2.4.   ERCOT’s Own Assertions of Engineering

2.4.1. On July 25, 2024, ERCOT filed its Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP)
       with the Public Utility Commission in Project No. 55718 (Item 17). The
       cover letter states: “ERCOT’s preparation of the Permian Basin Reliability
       Plan represents the culmination of a significant engineering effort (italics
       added) undertaken by ERCOT System Planning Staff”. The report states that
       “ERCOT conducted extensive engineering analysis” (italics added). The
       cover letter is signed by Kristi Hobbs, Vice President, System Planning &
       Weatherization.

                                         13
 2.4.2. The PBRP evaluated 345-kV, 500-kV and 765-kV import-path options and
       identified the specific facilities each would require. The 765-kV option
       consists of “Three new 765-kV single-circuit import paths” and
       “Approximately 1,255 miles of new 765-kV single-circuit transmission lines
       in total”. The Commission approved the plan in October 2024 and, on April
       24, 2025, approved “the three 765-kilovolt (kV) import paths identified in
       Table 7.5 of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan”.

2.4.3. On August 12, 2026, ERCOT wrote to Representative Charlie Geren that its
       planning process “relies on engineering studies” (italics added), that the
       PBRP “concluded that adding 765-kV facilities to the system provided the
       optimal engineering solution (italics added) for meeting reliability needs,”
       and that “The results of all three studies demonstrated, based on NERC
       reliability standards, the need for 765-kV additions to the system beginning
       in 2030.” (The three studies were the PBRP, the 2024 Regional Transmission
       Plan and the 2025 Regional Transmission Plan.) The letter concludes that
       ERCOT’s recommendation “reflects extensive engineering analysis (italics
       added) of multiple load scenarios” and that “765-kV facilities are the
       optimal engineering option” (italics added). It is signed by D. Woody
       Rickerson, ERCOT’s Senior Vice President and Chief Operating Officer, a
       licensed professional engineer in Texas PE 83379, without a “P.E.”
       designation.

2.4.4. ERCOT’s public declarations of engineering attempt to yield the credibility
       of engineering analyses to potentially unsuspecting people without such
       analyses actually having been credibly performed. Saying it’s engineered
       when it’s not per the Law is categorically wrong, and cannot be relied upon
       in any significant fashion..

2.4.5. The answer to the fourth question, “Does ERCOT assert that these Plans
       were derived using engineering?” is yes.

2.4.6. The answer to the fifth question, “Are the above Plans required or
       expected to contain the authenticity and the accountability of engineering
       works?” is yes.

2.5.   Statutory requirements for ERCOT Firm Registration

2.5.1. Under Texas Occupations Code § 1001.405(b) and 22 TAC § 137.77, a
       business entity may not engage in the practice of engineering in Texas
                                         14
       unless the entity is registered with TBPELS and designates an engineer in
      responsible charge. ERCOT is not registered as an engineering firm and
      holds no firm certificate ("F-number") on the TBPELS registry.

2.5.2. Under 22 TAC § 137.33, even preliminary engineering documents must
       clearly display the engineering firm name, the firm registration number, the
       person in responsible charge, and a conspicuous disclaimer stating that the
       document is preliminary.

2.5.3. A review of the PBRP, the 2024 RTP, and the 2025 RTP demonstrates
       complete non-compliance:

2.5.3.1. None of these reports are signed or sealed by a Texas licensed
         Professional Engineer.

2.5.3.2. None of these reports identify a designated Professional Engineer in
         responsible charge.

2.5.3.3. None of these reports bear a TBPELS firm registration number.

2.5.3.4. None of these reports display the mandatory preliminary engineering
         disclaimers.

2.5.4. Exemptions for the Practice of Engineering

2.5.4.1. ERCOT does not qualify for the private corporation exemption set forth
         in Texas Occupations Code § 1001.057, which exempts regular full-time
         employees of a private business entity only when engaged in:

      •   Reasonable modifications to existing buildings, facilities, or fixtures to
          real property that are not accessible to the general public and are owned,
          leased, or occupied by the entity; or
      •   Activities related strictly to the research, development, design,
          fabrication, production, assembly, integration, or service of manufactured
          products.

2.5.4.2. ERCOT is not a manufacturing entity, and its transmission reliability
         studies are not confined to its internal corporate offices. ERCOT's
         planning studies direct the construction of EHV transmission lines


                                         15
            crossing thousands of parcels of private and public land across the State
           of Texas.

2.5.4.3. ERCOT is not exempt under Texas Occupations Code § 1001.058
         ("Employee of Certain Utilities or Affiliates"), which provides a narrow
         exemption for regular full-time employees of a "privately owned public
         utility or cooperative utility" if the employee:

       •   Performs services exclusively for the utility or affiliate; and
       •   Does not have final authority to approve, or ultimate responsibility for,
           engineering designs, plans, or specifications that are to be:
              o incorporated into fixed works, systems, or facilities on the property
                 of others; or
              o (B) made available to the public.


2.5.4.4. ERCOT does not meet exemption requirements of § 1001.058:

       • ERCOT is an independent system operator certified under PURA §
         39.151—it is neither an investor-owned public utility nor an electric
         cooperative.
       • Even if ERCOT were treated as an affiliate of market utilities, its
         planning documents (the PBRP, the 2024 RTP, and the 2025 RTP) are
         published directly to the public and filed in regulatory dockets to justify
         CCN applications.
       • These Plans require engineering and are created with the intent to be
         incorporated into permanent high-voltage fixed works and transmission
         infrastructure situated on the property of private Texas landowners.

2.5.5. The subject Plans are anonymous institutional staff compilations. No
       licensed individual has applied their professional license or legal
       accountability on the accuracy, methodology, or validity of the power-flow
       models underpinning Import Path 2.

       Taken with the above, the Plans would appear to constitute the unlicensed
       practice of engineering.

2.5.6. The answer to the fifth question, “Is ERCOT required to be a registered
       firm in accordance with TBPELS rules?” is yes.

2.6.   Authority of the ALJs
                                          16
 2.6.1. The ALJs have the authority and duty to address this statutory failure. While
       SOAH Order No. 35 declined to order an independent technical audit of
       ERCOT because SOAH lacks self-initiating regulatory power, the ALJs
       possess authority under Texas Government Code § 2003.049 and 16 TAC §
       22.202 to determine the legal competency, admissibility, and weight of
       evidence on remand. The ALJs must determine whether the Applicants have
       satisfied their burden of proof through legally competent and credible
       substantial evidence.

2.6.2. Texas Occupations Code § 1001.553 establishes an affirmative statutory
       duty:

       "A public official of this state or of a political subdivision of this state shall
       report a violation of this chapter to the Board."

       Administrative Law Judges are public officials of Texas. If the ALJs
       determine that ERCOT is performing unexempt engineering studies without
       firm registration, and distributing unsealed engineering reports, the ALJs
       have an express statutory obligation to report ERCOT to TBPELS for formal
       enforcement action.

2.6.3. The answer to the seventh question, “Is the SOAH obliged to refer
       apparent engineering licensure and accountability questions to the TBPELS
       for investigation?” is yes.

2.7.   Ethical Obligations of the Commissioners

2.7.1. An unsealed, unregistered engineering report cannot serve as credible
       substantial evidence to support an administrative finding of public necessity
       under PURA § 37.056. The proper analogy is rooted in Texas administrative
       and municipal law governing building permits, public works, and
       environmental regulation.

2.7.2. Under Texas Occupations Code § 1001.402 ("Enforcement by Certain
       Public Officials"):

       "A public official of the state or of a political subdivision of the state who is
       responsible for enforcing laws that affect the practice of engineering may
       accept a plan, specification, or other related document only if the plan,

                                            17
       specification, or other document was prepared by an engineer, as evidenced
      by the engineer's seal."

2.7.3. The Texas Attorney General confirmed the mandatory nature of this statute
       in Opinion No. GA-0274 (2004), concluding that state and local officials
       have an affirmative duty to reject engineering submissions that fail to
       comply with TEPA's sealing and firm registration mandates.

2.7.4. The Applicants ask the Commission to grant CCN amendments authorizing
       hundreds of miles of 765-kV transmission lines costing many tens of billions
       of ratepayer dollars-and conferring eminent domain authority over private
       property-based entirely on unsealed, unauthenticated purported engineering
       analyses prepared by an unregistered corporation. Allowing unsealed
       planning studies to serve as credible substantial evidence would nullify the
       engineering consumer-protection laws established by the Texas Legislature.
       Unsealed engineering reports possess zero probative value and cannot
       support an affirmative finding on Preliminary Order Issue 11.

2.7.5. A direct ethical burden rests upon the Public Utility Commissioners,
       specifically Commissioner Kathleen Jackson, P.E., a registered Professional
       Engineer in the State of Texas.

2.2    NERC Mandates

Evaluating whether a transmission line is necessary to meet federal reliability
standards requires examining North American Electric Reliability Corporation
(NERC) Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1 ("Transmission System Planning
Performance Requirements") and its supporting Modeling, Data, and Analysis
(MOD) standards.

Federal reliability compliance is not an abstract policy projection; it is a
mandatory , calculations - driven engtneertng process governed by federal law
pursuant to 16 U.S.C. 8240. That statute's sole purpose is to enforce highly
technical math and physics-based engineering standards across the nation's power
grid..

2.2.1. Requirement Rl ofNERC TPL-001-5.1 obligates the Planning Coordinator
       (ERCOT) and Transmission Planners to maintain mathematical system
       models of the interconnected transmission network. The maintenance of
      these models carries the implicit requirement that the models use data
      consistently throughout the respective grid. These models must represent
      projected system conditions, real and reactive load demands, generation
      resources , safe operating limits , and physical transmission topologies ( i . e .,
      engineering) consistent with data submittals mandated by NERC Standard
      MOD-032-1.

2 . 2 . 2 . Requirement R.2 requires planners to conduct comprehensive steady - state
            power-flow simulations, dynamic angular stability analyses, and short-
             circuit interrupting duty calculations across a wide range of contingency
            Planning Events PO through P7 (f. e ., engineering). Planners must stress
             system models through sensitivity analyses that vary real and reactive load
            forecasts, dispatch patterns, and transfer levels (again, engineering).


                                            10
 2.2.3. Requirements R5 and R6 dictate that the planner establish quantitative
       criteria for steady -state bus voltage limits , transient voltage recovery, and
       system instability thresholds, including cascading failures and uncontrolled
       islanding (i.e., engineering).

2.2.4. Requirements R.2.7 and R.2.8 require that whenever simulations demonstrate
       thermal overloads or voltage instability, the planning entity must develop a
       formal Corrective Action Plan (CAP). A CAP specfies the precisephysical
       modification, replacement, or installation of high-voltage transmission
       lines, transformers, and switchgear necessary to maintain bulk electric
       system performance within safe physical margins (again, engineering).

2.2.5. Complementing these requirements:

2.2.5.1.   Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Standard MOD-033-1
           mandates the empirical validation of dynamic and steady-state planning
